questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what institutional trust is directed at rather than at political actors
questions.stem: A translator's note asks which term should be used when a respondent says they trust the courts to be fair, without mentioning any judge or party.

options.text: Institutional trust, because the object is the court as a body rather than a person
Vote intention, because a view about courts signals a future electoral choice
options.misconception: reads institutional confidence as an electoral preference

options.text: Political efficacy, because trusting courts expresses a sense of personal influence
options.misconception: confuses confidence in an institution with felt influence

options.text: Civic knowledge, because knowing the courts are fair shows factual understanding
options.misconception: treats a favourable judgement as a factual one

questions.explanation: Institutional trust attaches to the body rather than to the person who occupies it, so a respondent who names no judge or party is expressing trust in an institution. The alternatives misattribute the statement to elections, to personal influence or to factual knowledge.
questions.hint: Ask what the respondent named, a person or a body.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the connection between civic knowledge and political participation
questions.stem: In a translator's note, explain why civic knowledge and political participation are treated as two ends of a reinforcing relationship.

answer.exemplar: Civic knowledge is the store of facts a person holds about parties, institutions and policy options, and it tells them which course of action is available and what it might achieve. Participation then supplies feedback, because people who vote, campaign or attend meetings learn what institutions actually do, which corrects and extends their store of facts. The relationship therefore runs in both directions, and a policy or programme that raises knowledge without giving anyone something to do with it tends to leave participation flat.

questions.explanation: The item tests the two-way link between knowing how politics works and taking part in it, rather than treating knowledge as a one-way prerequisite. Participation generates the experience that corrects the knowledge in the first place.
questions.hint: Ask where participation sends its feedback.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role a policy entrepreneur plays in carrying a proposal

stimulus.body: A translation memo reports that a named official drafted the reform years before it became popular, kept a version ready in a drawer, and used a period of political crisis to press it on colleagues who had no interest in it. The memo asks what term the translator should use for that official.

questions.stem: Given the memo, which term best describes the official described?

options.text: A policy analyst, since the work consisted of producing research for others to use
options.misconception: reduces advocacy to producing analysis

options.text: A policy entrepreneur, since the official invested effort in promoting a proposal beyond its own office
A technical expert, since the proposal required specialised knowledge of the system
options.misconception: assumes expertise explains persistence of effort

options.text: A spokesperson, since the official communicated the government's settled position
options.misconception: treats advocacy of a new idea as communication of an old one

questions.explanation: The memo describes someone who invests sustained effort in promoting a specific proposal, keeps it ready and uses opportunity to push it, which is the defining behaviour of a policy entrepreneur. The alternatives describe analysis, expertise or communication, none of which requires the advocacy work described.
questions.hint: Ask what the official did with the proposal over time.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare universal and targeted programme design

stimulus.body: A margin note records that a subsidy was offered to every household without asking anyone's income, and that uptake was high. A second note records that a comparable scheme for the same group required proof of low income, that verification consumed most of its budget, and that many eligible households never applied.

questions.stem: Taking the margin notes together, what do they show about universal and targeted design?

options.text: Universal schemes are cheaper because they need no eligibility machinery
options.misconception: ignores that a universal benefit still has to be paid for everyone

options.text: Targeting always reaches more eligible people than a universal scheme
options.misconception: contradicts the note on take-up and verification cost

options.text: Targeting cuts the number of recipients but raises administrative cost and reduces take-up
The notes show the two designs differ only in how generous the benefit is
options.misconception: reduces the comparison to benefit size rather than administration

questions.explanation: Targeting narrows eligibility but adds verification work and, as the second note shows, that work can cost most of the budget and deter eligible people from applying. The universal scheme avoids the machinery and reaches far more of the intended group, at the price of paying non-poor households too.
questions.hint: Compare the cost side, not only the coverage side.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how veto players produce delay in decision-making
questions.stem: The translator's introduction argues that a proposal must clear a constitutional court and a second chamber before it takes effect. Which explanation of delay fits that arrangement?

options.text: Each body has an interested veto, so the delay comes from defending the proposal
options.misconception: misreads a blocking power as a supportive one

options.text: Each body can amend the proposal, so the delay comes from rewriting the text
options.misconception: confuses the ability to amend with the ability to refuse

options.text: Each body can summon further evidence, so the delay comes from gathering information
options.misconception: invents a procedural power the case never mentions

options.text: Each body can refuse assent, so the proposal's timetable is set by the slowest of them

questions.explanation: A veto player is an actor who can prevent a decision from taking effect, and each additional such actor lengthens the chain a proposal must clear. Here the court and the chamber can both refuse assent, so the slowest of them sets the timetable.
questions.hint: Ask which body can stop the decision outright.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify what opens the second window for policy change
questions.stem: A glossary entry in the translated edition defines a term for the moment when the political context finally becomes favourable to a long-prepared reform.

options.text: The first window, when the problem first becomes visible and urgent
options.misconception: confuses the recognition of the problem with political opportunity

options.text: The second window, when the politics window opens and a ready proposal can be pushed through
The policy window, when the problem has been defined but no solution exists yet
options.misconception: assumes opportunity arrives before any solution is prepared

options.text: The implementation window, when delivery begins and results start to appear
options.misconception: looks for the window after the decision has been taken

questions.explanation: The first window opens when a problem is recognised and gains attention, while the second opens when the political context turns favourable, giving advocates their chance to press a solution. A proposal that was not prepared during the first window is usually lost when the second one opens.
questions.hint: Ask which window concerns political opportunity.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why bargaining produces incremental rather than transformative change
questions.stem: In a translator's note, explain why negotiated bargaining between opposed parties tends to produce incremental rather than far-reaching change.

answer.exemplar: Bargaining advances only where the parties can each expect to gain something, and that mutual-gain zone is usually narrow when the dispute is partisan and the gains at stake are zero-sum in appearance. Even where both sides could be better off together, they must each be convinced they will not be the loser, and they must conceal their true preferences to do so. Because the achievable overlap is small and information about it is incomplete, the safest and most credible agreement is a modest step, and a series of such steps accumulates as incremental change.

questions.explanation: The item tests why negotiated agreement settles for small common gains rather than a wholesale settlement, since each side must be certain it will not end up worse off. The result is a sequence of modest steps rather than a single transformative bargain.
questions.hint: Ask how large the zone of mutual gain actually is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Name the three families of policy instrument

stimulus.body: A source excerpt lists three ways a government can steer behaviour. It names a transfer that changes what an action costs, a notice that changes what an actor knows, and a rule that changes what an actor is permitted to do. The excerpt notes that the same objective can be pursued through any of the three.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, which set of instrument families is being described?

options.text: Central, regional and local measures of government action
options.misconception: classifies instruments by the level of government that uses them

options.text: Legislative, judicial and executive measures of government action
options.misconception: classifies instruments by the branch that uses them

options.text: Financial measures, information measures and regulatory measures
Coercive, persuasive and payment measures of government action
options.misconception: treats the three families as a single dimension of force

questions.explanation: The excerpt names cost, knowledge and permission, which correspond to financial, information and regulatory instruments respectively. The alternatives regroup the same instruments by institution or by level, which says nothing about how an instrument actually shapes behaviour.
questions.hint: Look at what each instrument changes for the actor.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why institutional trust is specific to an object

stimulus.body: A margin note records that respondents said they trusted the courts but not the police, and that they trusted the police to enforce parking rules but not to handle complaints about conduct. The translator asks for a word that captures this pattern.

questions.stem: What does the margin note show about the trust described?

options.text: Trust is a fixed trait of each respondent that does not vary by institution
options.misconception: assumes a personal disposition rather than a relational judgement

options.text: Trust is a general feeling that applies to public bodies and is easily summarised
options.misconception: erases the differences the note records

options.text: Trust is simply a measure of whether people have had a recent bad experience
options.misconception: reduces institutional trust to personal contact with officials

options.text: Trust attaches to a specific institution and to a specific function, so it can differ across both

questions.explanation: The note shows trust varying both by body and by what the body is being trusted to do, which is exactly what object-specific trust means and why it cannot be summarised as one general feeling. The alternative that treats it as personal contact ignores cases where trust is general.
questions.hint: Ask which body and which task the trust attaches to.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a claim that information alone raises participation
questions.stem: After a leaflet explaining how to vote is sent to every household, turnout rises slightly and then returns to its former level. Which appraisal is best founded?

options.text: The leaflet failed entirely, since any rise in turnout shows the information had no effect
options.misconception: dismisses a measurable effect as if it were zero

options.text: Information helped only briefly, so the missing ingredient is likely the opportunity and reason to act
Turnout is a poor measure, so nothing can be concluded from the leaflet result
options.misconception: discards a usable indicator without reason

options.text: Turnout will rise further if the same leaflet is sent twice a year
options.misconception: assumes repetition fixes a structural obstacle

questions.explanation: A short-lived rise shows the leaflet informed people who were already willing to act, while the return to the previous level indicates the change ran out of people to reach. The obstacle therefore lies in opportunity and motivation rather than in the absence of information.
questions.hint: Separate the brief effect from the lasting one.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify the strategies available to a policy entrepreneur
questions.stem: The translation team must gloss a term for someone who champions a reform and decides whether to build support inside the organisation or outside it.

options.text: Ombudsman, who investigates complaints rather than promoting a specific reform
options.misconception: confuses scrutiny with sponsorship of a proposal

options.text: Bureaucrat, who must always work through formal internal procedures only
options.misconception: assumes internal strategy is the only lawful route

options.text: Policy entrepreneur, who may pursue inside or outside strategies and must assemble a coalition
Regulator, who applies rules that already exist rather than proposing new ones
options.misconception: treats rule making and rule enforcement as the same activity

questions.explanation: The defining features are championing a specific proposal, using inside or outside routes depending on the situation, and assembling a coalition that supports it. The other terms describe distinct institutional roles that do not centre on promoting a new idea.
questions.hint: Focus on the act of promoting a proposal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the trade-off between reach and cost in programme design
questions.stem: Explain, in the translator's note, why the choice between a universal and a targeted scheme is a trade-off rather than a question of which is better.

answer.exemplar: A universal scheme pays everyone in the eligible group and needs no eligibility test, so it reaches most of the people it is meant to help, but the total cost is the largest and some of the payment goes to households that did not need it. A targeted scheme aims the payment at the group that needs it and can therefore spend less per useful pound, but it must build and run an eligibility test, and the test costs money, delays payment and puts some eligible people off applying. Neither design dominates, since one trades breadth for administrative economy and the other trades economy for breadth.

questions.explanation: The item tests that the two designs optimise different things, so neither is simply the better choice. A design that pays only the needy saves money but loses people to the cost and friction of the test.
questions.hint: Ask what each design gives up in order to gain something.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the benefits a veto player can provide

stimulus.body: A translation memo describes a system in which any single court can strike down a regulation, and notes that the process has delayed three reforms that later proved unwise. The memo also records that two measures were blocked that would have allowed a minister to bypass safety rules without parliamentary approval.

questions.stem: According to the memo, what is the most balanced reading of the system's record?

options.text: The power to block works well in practice, since the three delayed reforms show the system operates as intended
options.misconception: treats delay of a flawed reform as evidence of good operation

options.text: The power to block is purely beneficial, since every measure it stopped turned out to be harmful
options.misconception: ignores the reforms the memo says later proved unwise

options.text: The power to block is purely costly, since blocking measures only ever delays reform
options.misconception: ignores the blocked measures that protected parliamentary approval

options.text: The power to block costs time and can delay good policy, while it also prevents concentrated and unchecked authority

questions.explanation: The memo records both costs, in the reforms delayed and later regretted, and benefits, in blocking measures that removed parliamentary scrutiny. A reading that takes only one side drops half of the evidence the memo supplies.
questions.hint: The memo supplies evidence on both sides.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply the window concept to a missed opportunity

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that a commission reported on a problem in a year of loud public criticism and recommended a particular remedy. The note continues that the government was busy with a financial crisis, the recommended remedy was set aside, and when attention returned two years later the report was treated as history rather than as a live proposal.

questions.stem: According to the translator's note, why was the recommended remedy never adopted?

options.text: The commission misidentified the problem, so the remedy had nothing to work on
options.misconception: implies the note reports a diagnostic failure

options.text: The political opportunity passed while no one was positioned to press the remedy at that moment
The remedy was too expensive for the budget of the period
options.misconception: adds a cost explanation the note never raises

options.text: The public stopped caring about the problem once the crisis began
options.misconception: misreads the crisis as a loss of attention to the issue

questions.explanation: The commission's report opened the first window by defining the problem and recommending a remedy, but the politics window closed or never opened, and with no advocate ready to press the remedy at that moment the proposal lapsed. The later treatment of the report as history is the standard consequence of a missed second window.
questions.hint: Ask who was positioned to act when the opening came.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the claim that incrementalism always produces better outcomes
questions.stem: A long series of negotiated steps fixes several grievances but leaves a rule that produces the underlying problem untouched. Which appraisal is best founded?

options.text: Incrementalism succeeded fully, since the negotiated steps removed every source of grievance
options.misconception: contradicts the premise about the rule left untouched

options.text: Incrementalism failed, since it did not remove the rule that caused the grievances
options.misconception: sets a single standard of success and applies it to all change

options.text: Incrementalism delivered real gains but also entrenched the arrangement, so its effects cut both ways
The steps show negotiation is the wrong method, since only structural change settles problems
options.misconception: infers a general verdict from one case

questions.explanation: The negotiated steps did resolve the specific grievances they addressed, so incrementalism can produce real gains, yet they also built vested interests around a rule that still causes the problem. The evidence supports a mixed judgement rather than a verdict either way.
questions.hint: Ask what the sequence achieved and what it entrenched.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Select an appropriate instrument type for a stated objective
questions.stem: A translation team must choose an instrument for a case where households do not know that a benefit they are owed exists.

options.text: A regulatory measure, since the administrative authority should verify eligibility more strictly
options.misconception: reads missing awareness as a need for tighter checks

options.text: A financial measure, since paying more always fixes a lack of awareness
options.misconception: assumes a payment would make an uninformed household claim

options.text: A regulatory measure, since the benefit should be made compulsory so that no one can refuse it
options.misconception: confuses providing a benefit with requiring acceptance of it

options.text: An information measure, since the obstacle is what households know rather than what they can afford

questions.explanation: The stated obstacle is that eligible households do not know the benefit exists, which is a problem of information rather than of price or permission, so an information measure addresses it directly. Paying more would not help households who never apply, and tightening checks would add friction without informing anyone.
questions.hint: Ask what the obstacle actually is.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the consequence of low institutional trust for compliance
questions.stem: Explain, in the translator's note, why low institutional trust makes voluntary compliance with official rules harder to sustain.

answer.exemplar: Voluntary compliance rests on the belief that the rule is legitimate and that applying it will be fair and consistent. Where trust in the enforcing institution is low, people have good reason to expect arbitrary or corrupt treatment, so they privately conclude that paying or complying buys them nothing they can rely on. Two effects follow. Evasion rises, because the expected gain from avoiding the rule outweighs the expected loss from being caught, and where a scheme needs self-reporting, non-reporting rises with it. Trust is therefore a practical condition of compliance rather than a moral nicety.

questions.explanation: The item tests the link between institutional trust and voluntary compliance, which runs through expectations about how the rule will be enforced. Low trust raises the expected payoff from evasion and discourages the self-reporting that schemes depend on.
questions.hint: Ask what a person expects to get for complying.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Read a source that distinguishes knowledge from resources

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes an information campaign that raised measured knowledge of the electoral system across all income groups, and reports that participation rose only among those with free time and money to take part. The excerpt asks the translator to avoid rendering the campaign as a failure.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what is the most accurate account of the campaign's effect?

options.text: The campaign failed, since participation did not rise across all income groups
options.misconception: ignores the knowledge gain the campaign plainly produced

options.text: The campaign removed the knowledge barrier evenly, while unequal resources still shaped who could act on it
The campaign succeeded fully, since knowledge and participation are the same thing
options.misconception: collapses the two variables the excerpt separates

options.text: Resources are irrelevant to participation, since the rise in participation proves the point
options.misconception: contradicts the excerpt's finding about money and time

questions.explanation: The excerpt separates the two variables: knowledge rose for everyone while participation rose only where money and time made acting possible. That is a partial success with an unequal distribution of benefit, not a failure and not a complete one.
questions.hint: The excerpt gives you two separate findings.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a policy entrepreneur from a policy champion

stimulus.body: A translator's note describes one official who kept a reform alive for eleven years by adjusting it to fit each incoming minister, and a second official who blocked the same reform twice by organising opposition among the departments it would have affected. The note asks whether both should be rendered with the same term.

questions.stem: Should the two officials described be given the same term?

options.text: Yes, because any sustained attention to a proposal makes someone its entrepreneur
options.misconception: defines the role so loosely it covers everyone

options.text: Yes, because both are officials who influenced the outcome of the same reform
options.misconception: collapses opposition and sponsorship into one role

options.text: No, because the first promotes a proposal while the second works to prevent one, which is a different relationship to policy
No, because only elected officials may act on policy in this way
options.misconception: invents an electoral requirement the note does not mention

questions.explanation: The first official champions a proposal and works to keep it alive, while the second systematically obstructs one, and the relationship to the policy is opposite in each case. Sharing a subject of attention does not make the two roles the same.
questions.hint: Ask which one is promoting the reform.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the equity effects of programme targeting
questions.stem: A targeted scheme pays more per recipient than a universal one and reaches fewer of the intended group. Which judgement about fairness is most defensible?

options.text: Fairness cannot be judged here, since no distributional data are given
options.misconception: declares the question unanswerable rather than weighing the evidence

options.text: The universal scheme is automatically fairer, since it treats everyone identically
options.misconception: mistakes identical treatment for equal outcome

options.text: The targeted scheme is automatically fairer, since money for the poor is always better value
options.misconception: assumes targeted spending always helps poor households more

options.text: Equity depends on who ends up better off overall, so the higher spend per person and lower reach must both be weighed

questions.explanation: Fairness turns on the distribution of benefit across households, so a judgement has to weigh the larger payment per recipient against the smaller number actually reached and the people left out. Identical treatment and value per pound are separate arguments that do not settle distributional outcomes.
questions.hint: Weigh reach and amount, not just one of them.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the number of veto players affects policy stability
questions.stem: A translator's note must gloss a passage comparing a country where one actor can block a decision against one where five separate actors can each block it.

options.text: The country with more veto players has more stable policy, since agreement requires wider consent
options.misconception: mistakes the difficulty of agreement for its durability

options.text: The country with more veto players faces more delay and less stable policy, since more gates must be passed
Both countries face the same delay, since a single block is as decisive as five
options.misconception: ignores that each additional gate adds chances to stop

options.text: The difference reflects the size of the country rather than the number of blocking actors
options.misconception: invents a size explanation the note does not raise

questions.explanation: Each additional actor who can block adds another opportunity for a decision to stall, so policy in a country with many veto players is less stable and slower to settle. Wider consent may make an outcome more durable once reached, but the route to it is longer.
questions.hint: Ask how many chances exist to stop a decision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how problem and politics windows combine
questions.stem: Explain, in the translator's note, how the two windows for policy change combine and why a proposal must be ready for both.

answer.exemplar: Two openings have to coincide. The first window opens when a problem is defined and gains attention, usually after a crisis or a report, which creates the demand for action. The second window opens later, when the political context changes, for instance an election, a change of minister or a crisis elsewhere, and creates an opportunity to press a solution. A proposal that is ready only during the first window arrives without a solution, and one that arrives during the second without having been prepared is usually overtaken by events. Advocates therefore keep a developed option in reserve so that it can be pressed at once.

questions.explanation: The item tests that both openings must coincide and that preparation done in the wrong window is wasted. Keeping a developed option ready is what allows a solution to be pressed the moment the political opening arrives.
questions.hint: Ask when the solution must be ready.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how bargaining can produce mutual gains

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a settlement in which each side received the item it valued most and conceded the item it valued least, and notes that the parties had disagreed publicly before the talks and remained cordial afterwards. The excerpt adds that the same dispute had once been described as a zero-sum contest over a single asset.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what made the settlement possible?

options.text: Public disagreement had damaged the parties' standing, so pressure forced them to the table
options.misconception: invents a reputational cause the excerpt does not state

options.text: One side simply conceded, so the outcome was a victory for the stronger party
options.misconception: replaces a trade between equals with a one-sided defeat

options.text: The items the parties valued were not identical, so a trade gave each side more than the zero-sum fight would have
The asset was split into pieces, so each side received half of what it wanted
options.misconception: misdescribes a trade of different items as a division of one

questions.explanation: Bargaining can create mutual gains because what each side values is rarely the same thing, so exchanging the least-valued item for the most-valued one leaves both better off. The excerpt's note that the dispute was once seen as zero-sum shows why the trade was available only once the items were separated.
questions.hint: Ask what each side actually valued.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the choice of instrument determines how behaviour responds

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that a rise in a tax on sugary drinks was followed by a sharp fall in purchases, while a publicity campaign about the same drink produced a rise in discussions and almost no change in sales. The note records that the two measures ran in different years and different regions.

questions.stem: Taking the translator's note into account, what does the difference in results show?

options.text: Both measures worked, since more discussion about a drink is a form of purchase avoidance
options.misconception: equates conversation with behaviour change

options.text: The publicity failed because campaigns never work when taxes are low
options.misconception: invents a tax threshold rule from a single comparison

options.text: The tax worked only because the same regions had received publicity first
options.misconception: adds a sequencing effect the note does not report

options.text: Financial and regulatory measures change the cost of an action directly, while information measures shape what people know

questions.explanation: The tax altered the price of an action and people responded, whereas the campaign altered what people knew and their purchases barely moved, which is exactly the difference the three instrument families imply. The note's qualification about years and regions also warns against reading more into the comparison than it supports.
questions.hint: Ask what each measure changed for the actor.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the consequences of distrust in government institutions
questions.stem: A community has low trust in local authorities yet high trust in a neighbourhood mutual aid group. Which analysis best holds both facts together?

options.text: Trust is a general trait, so the two ratings contradict each other and one is a mistake
options.misconception: forces one general feeling that the evidence contradicts

options.text: Trust attaches to specific objects, so confidence in one body says nothing about confidence in another
Trust rises with proximity, so the second rating is simply an artefact of distance
options.misconception: explains the pattern with proximity, which applies to both bodies equally

options.text: The second rating reflects liking rather than trust, so it does not count
options.misconception: excludes an answer by relabelling it without evidence

questions.explanation: Because trust is directed at particular objects, a person can hold the authorities in low regard while relying heavily on a local group they know, and the two ratings are perfectly compatible. The alternative that treats trust as one general feeling cannot accommodate the case at all.
questions.hint: Ask what trust is being spent on in each case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify who is most likely to be politically active and why
questions.stem: A translator's note describes a group that reads political news carefully, joins a local campaign and has money and time to spend on it. Another group reads little, has no money to spare and no free hours. Which group is more likely to take part?

options.text: Neither, since participation depends mainly on which political party a person supports
options.misconception: reduces participation to party preference

options.text: The second, because people with few resources are usually most eager to change matters
options.misconception: confuses economic pressure with capacity to act

options.text: The first, because knowledge and resources both raise the likelihood of participation
Both equally, since reading the news removes any difference in resources
options.misconception: assumes information substitutes for money and time

questions.explanation: Participation is more likely where people know how the system works and can afford the money and time it takes, which is exactly the combination the first group has. Reading the news does not create the hours or the funds that the second group lacks.
questions.hint: Ask what both knowledge and resources contribute.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a prepared proposal is needed at the moment of opportunity
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, why a policy entrepreneur keeps a developed proposal ready rather than writing it once attention arrives.

answer.exemplar: The moment of political opportunity is brief and usually arrives at a moment when attention is elsewhere, so there is no time to commission research, consult and draft a credible scheme. A proposal written during the window of opportunity is therefore never finished in time, and the window closes on an unfinished document. Advocates who keep a scheme developed and costed in reserve can present something workable the moment the context turns favourable, and they can also use the waiting years to build the coalition and the credibility that the proposal will need in order to be accepted.

questions.explanation: The item tests why readiness in advance matters, since the window of opportunity leaves no time for drafting. Preparation also builds the support and credibility the proposal will need once the moment arrives.
questions.hint: Ask how long the window stays open.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how eligibility tests can exclude eligible people

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a means-tested scheme where claimants must produce payslips or a certificate of residence, and where the forms are available only in paper form at an office open two afternoons a week. It records that a quarter of households in the area have no payslips and that the certificate takes six weeks to obtain.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, how does the eligibility test work against eligible people?

options.text: The paper form causes delays for everyone equally, so it does not affect who benefits
options.misconception: ignores the uneven distribution of paperwork capacity

options.text: The scheme pays too little, so eligible households decline the money on principle
options.misconception: invents a refusal that the excerpt does not report

options.text: The test is too generous, since too many households qualify for the benefit
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the problem the excerpt describes

options.text: The proof required is costly and slow to obtain, so people who qualify drop out before they ever claim

questions.explanation: Targeting pushes the burden of proof onto claimants, and where the documents are hard to obtain the rule filters out people who qualify, so the scheme reaches fewer of the intended group than its design implies. The exclusions fall on those with the least paperwork capacity.
questions.hint: Ask what the test demands of the applicant.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess delay as a strategic choice by a veto player

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that a reviewing court refused to rule on a regulation for eight months while the ministry was being reorganised, and that when it eventually ruled it upheld almost all of the regulation. The note also records that the court had no power to delay and no fixed deadline for its rulings.

questions.stem: What does the translator's note suggest about the delay?

options.text: The delay was unavoidable, since the ministry's reorganisation suspended all rulings automatically
options.misconception: invents a suspension rule the note does not record

options.text: The delay came from the court's own discretion, so it was a choice to wait rather than a mechanical rule
The delay shows the court opposed the regulation and was delaying to obstruct it
options.misconception: infers opposition from timing that ended in approval

options.text: The delay proves the regulation was legally sound, since a court would not wait on sound rules
options.misconception: treats timing as a legal assessment

questions.explanation: Because the court had discretion over timing and no deadline, the eight-month gap reflects its own choice about when to rule rather than any procedure that compelled the wait. The eventual upholding of the regulation makes the obstruction reading hard to sustain.
questions.hint: Note whether the court was obliged to wait.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a window opening from a policy being adopted
questions.stem: A new minister arrives, the press discusses a long-neglected problem, and a well-prepared proposal is pressed immediately. It is reported as a policy win. What does the window account add?

options.text: The opening means the problem was solved earlier without anyone noticing it
options.misconception: misreads attention as a prior solution

options.text: The opening settles the matter, since a prepared proposal is normally adopted without further resistance
options.misconception: treats opportunity as adoption

options.text: The opening created the chance, but the proposal still had to be pressed, won and implemented by others
The opening invalidates the preparation, since the proposal should have been written in response to the new minister
options.misconception: claims prior preparation is a disadvantage

questions.explanation: A window supplies the opportunity and makes the effort of advocates worthwhile, but it does not itself carry a proposal through adoption, which requires persuasion, a decision and delivery. Readiness improves the odds of success without removing the need to win support.
questions.hint: Separate chance from outcome.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how incrementalism can entrench existing arrangements
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how a run of small negotiated settlements can make a much larger change harder rather than easier.

options.text: Each settlement slows the economy, which makes governments reluctant to move faster
options.misconception: invents an economic effect the note never mentions

options.text: Each settlement reduces the total amount at stake, so there is less left to disagree about
options.misconception: assumes shrinking stakes make agreement harder

options.text: Each settlement removes one policy option from the table, so the choice space narrows
options.misconception: describes a narrowing of choices rather than new stakes

options.text: Each settlement gives the parties a stake in the arrangement and makes further change harder to agree

questions.explanation: Incremental settlements hand participants something to lose, so a later, larger change now threatens gains they have already secured, which raises the price of agreement. The alternatives describe mechanisms the note does not support.
questions.hint: Ask what participants gain from each step.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why instrument choice mixes with other policy choices
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, why the choice of instrument is a political choice and not merely a technical one.

answer.exemplar: An instrument determines who bears the cost, who receives the benefit and how much discretion is left to the person being regulated. A financial instrument sets a price, which rewards those who can pay and punishes those who cannot, so it distributes burdens in a way the designer chooses. An information instrument leaves the choice with the target and relies on the target's capacity to respond, which rewards the better informed. A regulatory instrument removes the choice entirely and concentrates discretion in the enforcing authority. Because each of these builds a different distribution of costs and freedom, the instrument cannot be picked on technical grounds alone.

questions.explanation: The item tests that instruments carry distributional and discretionary consequences, so picking one is a political act. Treating instrument choice as purely technical misses who pays and who decides.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost and who keeps discretion.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how trust in institutions differs from satisfaction with performance

stimulus.body: A source excerpt reports that people rated the local council's performance in handling waste poorly, and separately reported that they did not trust the council to be honest about its finances. It records that trust in the same council rose in areas where officials published the underlying accounts.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what is the relationship between performance and trust?

options.text: They are the same thing, since poor performance necessarily destroys trust
options.misconception: collapses two different judgements into one

options.text: They are distinct, and trust can respond to openness about how decisions are taken rather than to the outcome itself
Trust is unaffected by performance because it is built entirely from a sense of national identity
options.misconception: invents an identity basis the excerpt never mentions

options.text: Trust follows performance closely, so the rise in trust shows the service must have improved
options.misconception: assumes a service improvement the excerpt does not record

questions.explanation: The excerpt reports poor performance and low trust as separate measures, and then shows trust responding to transparency about finances, which is a question of process rather than of service quality. That supports treating trust and satisfaction as distinct.
questions.hint: Note what the trust change followed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how participation builds civic knowledge
questions.stem: The translator flags a phrase and asks whether it should say that participation produces knowledge or that knowledge produces participation.

answer.exemplar: Both directions are real and the passage can legitimately state the relationship as reciprocal. Knowledge produces participation because people who do not know how the system works, who is responsible for what, or what an option would cost cannot choose sensibly or feel able to act. Participation produces knowledge because the experience of campaigning, voting and dealing with officials reveals what institutions actually do rather than what they are said to do, and it corrects the tentative impressions that come from reading alone. Translators who pick one direction alone will mislead an English reader about the argument.

questions.explanation: The item tests the reciprocal relationship and the risk of translating it as one-way. Participation supplies the experience that corrects what people previously believed about how institutions work.
questions.hint: Ask where the flow of information runs in each direction.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how coalition building supports a policy entrepreneur

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that an official changed the design of a proposal so that the departments that would lose funding could keep a transitional payment, and that the proposal then advanced without opposition. The note asks what word to use for what the official did.

questions.stem: What does the translator's note describe?

options.text: Convincing opponents that the original design was always the wrong policy
options.misconception: assumes the opponents changed their minds about the substance

options.text: Splitting the proposal into parts so that no single body could reject it
options.misconception: misreads the design change as a procedural device

options.text: Building a coalition by compensating potential opponents so that opposition is removed
Delaying the proposal until the funding dispute was settled by the finance ministry
options.misconception: invents a referral the note never records

questions.explanation: The official identified those who would lose from the proposal and gave them a reason not to oppose it, which is how coalitions are built by removing opposition rather than by persuasion alone. The alternatives describe tactics the note does not report.
questions.hint: Ask why the losing departments stayed quiet.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Compare how universal and targeted schemes affect coverage of the poor
questions.stem: A translator's note asks which design reaches a larger share of the households living on a low income.

options.text: Neither reaches them, since poor households avoid official schemes as a rule
options.misconception: generalises a barrier into a rule about all poor households

options.text: The targeted design, since it identifies low-income households precisely
options.misconception: ignores the gap between eligibility and successful claims

options.text: Both reach the same share, since the total budget is what limits coverage
options.misconception: assumes a fixed budget and equal outcomes from it

options.text: The universal design, since it reaches everyone without an eligibility test that many cannot pass

questions.explanation: A universal scheme reaches nearly all of the intended group because no applicant has to prove anything, while a targeted scheme only reaches those who both qualify and successfully complete the test, and the poorest households are often those least able to do the paperwork. Precision about who qualifies is not the same thing as reaching them.
questions.hint: Compare who applies with who qualifies.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish delay from blockage in veto player analysis
questions.stem: A translator's note distinguishes a decision held up for a year from a decision stopped outright. Which account best explains why the distinction matters?

options.text: The distinction matters only for scheduling, since both leave the eventual policy the same
options.misconception: assumes a modified proposal is the same as the original

options.text: Delay lets the proposal return in modified form, while blockage ends it, so the two have different consequences for policy
Delay is worse than blockage, since a stalled decision wastes more effort
options.misconception: ranks them by effort rather than by outcome

options.text: The distinction does not matter, since veto players who delay usually block later
options.misconception: asserts a regularity the note provides no evidence for

questions.explanation: A delay that merely slows a decision leaves the proposal alive and often returns it in an altered form, whereas a block ends it, and the two therefore lead to different policy outcomes. Treating them as equivalent removes the very distinction the note draws.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the proposal in each case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate why preparation improves the chance of success
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, why advocates who keep a scheme ready are more likely to succeed when the political opening finally arrives.

answer.exemplar: The political opening is short and unpredictable, and the attention that accompanies it is absorbed by whatever is newest, so a proposal that has to be created at that moment is unlikely to be finished, costed and supported in time. A scheme prepared in advance can be presented immediately, in finished and costed form, which lets its advocates use the attention rather than lose it. Preparation also does quieter work: it allows the coalition to be assembled, the credibility of the sponsor to be established, and the criticisms of opponents to be answered before anyone has the chance to make them.

questions.explanation: The item tests why readiness converts a rare opening into a real chance rather than a wasted occasion. Preparation buys time for consultation and coalition building that the window itself does not allow.
questions.hint: Ask what the advocates would otherwise have to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why incremental change can be easier to implement

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a negotiated settlement that reduced a contested subsidy by a small sum, kept every side's savings, and was then carried out without further argument. The excerpt contrasts it with a comprehensive settlement of the same question that had been abandoned three times over a decade.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, why was the small settlement carried out?

options.text: It was negotiated, so every participant accepted it without argument
options.misconception: assumes negotiation removes disagreement

options.text: It was smaller, so it cost the administration less to administer
options.misconception: invents a cost argument the excerpt does not make

options.text: It left every participant better off and settled, so implementation required nobody to reverse a commitment
It was negotiated, so it avoided the need for money to be found
options.misconception: mistakes a smaller change for a cost-free change

questions.explanation: The small settlement gave every side something it valued and required no participant to give up a visible gain, so once made nobody had a reason to reopen it. The earlier comprehensive bargains failed because they asked someone to bear the whole loss.
questions.hint: Ask whether anyone lost in the final settlement.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish instrument families from policy objectives
questions.stem: Two programmes pursue the same objective of reducing emissions, one through a price on fuel and one through a requirement to fit a filter. Which account best frames the choice?

options.text: The choice is between a financial and a regulatory objective, since instruments set aims
options.misconception: confuses the means with the end

options.text: The two programmes have different objectives, since only one of them addresses emissions directly
options.misconception: treats a shared aim as two aims

options.text: The two programmes are equivalent in effect, since both reduce the same activity
options.misconception: assumes identical instruments produce identical effects

options.text: The objective is the same while the instrument families differ, so the choice concerns price and permission rather than purpose

questions.explanation: The instrument families describe how a policy steers behaviour, not what it is trying to achieve, and the same objective can be pursued through price, information or permission with quite different distributional effects. The alternative that treats them as equivalent ignores the different burdens each places on households.
questions.hint: Separate the aim from the means.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall the difference between institutional trust and trust in representatives
questions.stem: A translator's note must distinguish trust in a court as an institution from trust in the particular judge who heard the case.

options.text: The two are the same, since a fair body is always staffed by fair judges
options.misconception: assumes staffing follows the institution's character automatically

options.text: Institutional trust concerns the body's rules and fairness, while personal trust concerns the individual judge
Only personal trust is legitimate, since institutions cannot be trusted by anyone
options.misconception: dismisses a well-established category

options.text: Only institutional trust matters politically, since judges are rarely elected
options.misconception: confuses relevance with legitimacy of the category

questions.explanation: Institutional trust attaches to the standing rules and fairness of the body, which persists across personnel, while personal trust attaches to the particular judge. The two can diverge, since a fair court may contain an untrustworthy individual judge.
questions.hint: Ask what the trust survives when the person changes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why resource inequalities shape political participation
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, why unequal resources translate into unequal political participation even when knowledge is equal.

answer.exemplar: Political activity costs money, time and sometimes risk, and these costs fall unevenly on households that have less of each. A person who works irregular hours, cannot afford transport and has caring responsibilities can be equally well informed as a neighbour yet unable to attend a meeting, fund a campaign or queue at a polling station with children to manage. Where the evidence shows equal knowledge but sharply unequal participation, the missing element is therefore the capacity to act on what is known, and remedies that supply information alone leave that gap where it was.

questions.explanation: The item tests that equal knowledge does not produce equal participation, because acting on political choices carries uneven money, time and risk costs. Information campaigns that ignore capacity cannot close the gap they set out to close.
questions.hint: Ask what participation costs besides knowledge.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the contribution of a policy entrepreneur to a reform

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a reform that was adopted after a particular official spent six years adjusting it to fit successive ministers, wrote the official's own draft when nobody else would, and assembled a group of outside supporters to carry the argument when the ministry lost interest. It notes that the reform was popular and that no other official had pressed the same case.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, how should the official's contribution be assessed?

options.text: The official was a technocrat whose drafting skill explains the reform's adoption
options.misconception: reduces a political contribution to technical drafting ability

options.text: The reform's popularity shows the official contributed little, since it would have passed without them
options.misconception: treats a popular outcome as proof of no individual contribution

options.text: The official converted an idea into an adopted reform by sustaining it, drafting it and building support
The ministry's loss of interest shows the official misjudged the proposal's support
options.misconception: treats a change of interest as evidence of error

questions.explanation: The excerpt attributes the passage from an idea to an adopted reform to the official's sustained advocacy, drafting and coalition work, which together is the substance of the role. Popularity of the outcome is not a measure of any one person's contribution to securing it.
questions.hint: Ask what would have happened without that work.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how targeting can create gaps between eligibility and entitlement

stimulus.body: A translator's note records a benefit that pays most of the cost of childcare for families earning below a stated income, and nothing for a family one unit above that income. It notes that several families are close to the threshold and that the income figures are revised only once a year.

questions.stem: According to the translator's note, what problem does the threshold create?

options.text: The threshold is a fair way to direct funds, since it separates those who need help from those who do not
options.misconception: accepts the fairness of a sharp drop without checking who bears it

options.text: The threshold makes total spending unpredictable, since the number of eligible families cannot be estimated
options.misconception: turns an equity problem into a budgeting one

options.text: The threshold encourages employers to raise wages to just under the line
options.misconception: invents an employer response the note does not report

options.text: Families just below the line lose far more than families just above it, so eligibility cliffs fall harshly on those near it

questions.explanation: A hard income threshold means a small change in circumstances can remove a large part of a family's support, so the cliff falls hardest on households whose income sits near the line. Whether a scheme is fair therefore depends on the size of the discontinuity, not only on who qualifies.
questions.hint: Compare two households on either side of the line.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the effects of veto players on policy quality
questions.stem: A translator's note records that in one country proposals take three times as long to pass as in another, and that the first country's laws contain fewer provisions that were later found to breach rights. Which account best explains both facts?

options.text: The two facts are unrelated, since slow countries cannot produce careful laws
options.misconception: denies a link the note supplies

options.text: The extra scrutiny costs time and filters out rights-violating provisions, so delay can buy quality
The first country has more lawyers, which explains both the delay and the legal quality
options.misconception: invents a professional cause the note never mentions

options.text: The first country passes fewer laws simply because it has less need to legislate
options.misconception: explains volume by need rather than by process

questions.explanation: The same feature, a wider set of actors who can block or require scrutiny, produces both the longer timetable and the removal of rights-violating provisions before enactment. Delay is therefore not simply a cost, and reading the two facts as unrelated misses the mechanism that links them.
questions.hint: Ask what one process could produce both results.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall what the first window represents
questions.stem: A glossary drafted for the translated edition needs to distinguish the two windows that open for policy change.

options.text: The first opens when a solution is drafted, the second when it is implemented
options.misconception: moves both openings into the process after the decision

options.text: The first opens when a government takes office, the second when a problem is first reported
options.misconception: swaps the two openings around

options.text: The first opens when a problem is defined and gains attention, the second when the politics become favourable
The two windows are the same opening observed by different analysts
options.misconception: collapses two distinct openings into one

questions.explanation: The first window is the moment a problem is defined and commands attention, and the second is the moment the political context turns favourable to acting on it. Their separation is what creates the need for advocates to prepare a solution in advance.
questions.hint: Ask which opening concerns attention and which concerns opportunity.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the link between bargaining and policy stability
questions.stem: Explain, in the translator's note, why bargaining produces stable policy that is hard to reverse.

answer.exemplar: A negotiated settlement is stable because every participant holds something they gained from it and would lose by reopening the question, so reversal would require everyone to surrender a secured gain rather than merely changing the subject. Stability is therefore built from the terms of the bargain rather than from any commitment to the underlying principle. The difficulty follows directly: because the arrangement is defended by the interests it created, later attempts to scale it up meet organised resistance from the very participants who helped make it work.

questions.explanation: The item tests why negotiated outcomes resist reversal, because each participant is defending an interest the bargain created. That same mechanism is what makes later, larger change difficult.
questions.hint: Ask what each participant would lose by reopening it.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of an information instrument

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a disclosure requirement forcing food sellers to publish the salt content of every item, and records that within a year the average salt content of prepared foods fell while sales of the disclosed high-salt items did not collapse. The excerpt notes that sellers had reformulated rather than raised prices.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, how does the disclosure requirement work?

options.text: It works through regulation of sellers, because sellers had to change what they were allowed to sell
options.misconception: reads a disclosure duty as a prohibition on products

options.text: It sets a price, because reformulation was achieved by adding cost to high-salt items
options.misconception: contradicts the note that prices did not rise

options.text: It limits high-salt items, because publication of their content functioned as a ban
options.misconception: confuses disclosure with prohibition

options.text: It changes what buyers and sellers know, which alters their choices without setting a price or a legal limit

questions.explanation: The requirement altered the information available to buyers and sellers, and the reformulation followed from that information reaching the market, not from a new price or a prohibition. Disclosure is the instrument that makes the content of goods knowable so that choices can shift.
questions.hint: Ask what the requirement made possible that was not possible before.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Apply object specificity to a trust scenario

stimulus.body: A translator's note records that people who say they trust the electoral commission complain about postal voting arrangements in the same surveys, and that a reviewer suggested the complaints show the trust is unreal. The note asks whether that reading holds.

questions.stem: Does the translator's note support the reviewer's reading that the trust is unreal?

options.text: Yes, because criticism of one procedure shows the general trust was never real
options.misconception: conflates specific feedback with the whole of a general trust

options.text: No, because trust in an institution's overall integrity can coexist with specific criticism of one procedure
No, because postal voting is not an electoral commission responsibility
options.misconception: denies the connection the note draws

options.text: Yes, because a single criticism is enough to withdraw trust in an institution
options.misconception: treats any dissent as full withdrawal of trust

questions.explanation: Trust in the body's overall integrity and a specific complaint about one of its procedures are compatible, and the second is often evidence that the trust is doing work by providing a channel for complaint. Reading the complaint as proof that the trust was never real discards the distinction between general and specific judgement.
questions.hint: Ask what a specific complaint implies about general trust.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the design of a participation programme
questions.stem: A programme offers online voting advice and public information sessions but holds no elections, no petitions and no meetings. Which appraisal is best founded?

options.text: The programme is well designed, because understanding politics is the main barrier to participation
options.misconception: ignores the absence of any opportunity to act

options.text: The programme will raise participation, since informed citizens always take part
options.misconception: assumes knowledge alone is sufficient for participation

options.text: The programme addresses knowledge while removing the chances to act, so it is unlikely to raise participation
The programme cannot be assessed, since participation figures are always contested
options.misconception: declares the evidence unusable without weighing it

questions.explanation: Since participation requires both the knowledge to choose and an opportunity to act, a programme that supplies only the first removes the very thing the second depends on. The appraisal therefore has to look at the whole design rather than at its informative parts.
questions.hint: Ask what the programme leaves people with no opportunity to do.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Recall the defining features of a policy entrepreneur
questions.stem: A glossary entry in the translation must list what sets a policy entrepreneur apart from an ordinary official or adviser.

options.text: A permanent post in one department, since mobility makes advocacy impossible
options.misconception: invents a staffing requirement not implied by the term

options.text: A senior rank, since only people near the top can champion a reform
options.misconception: ties the role to hierarchy rather than to behaviour

options.text: A technical specialism, since proposals need expertise to survive scrutiny
options.misconception: reduces advocacy to subject knowledge

options.text: A willingness to invest resources in a proposal and to use political opportunities to advance it

questions.explanation: What distinguishes the role is the sustained investment of effort and resources in a specific proposal and the use of political openings to advance it, not rank, expertise or job security. The other options import conditions the concept does not require.
questions.hint: Focus on what the person does with a proposal.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why universal programmes may be preferable in some circumstances
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, why universal design can be defended even where a targeted scheme would spend fewer pounds on the households that most need help.

answer.exemplar: Universal design avoids building an eligibility test, and the cost of that test in money, staff time and applicant burden is often a large share of the scheme's budget. It also avoids the exclusion that testing produces, since households without the required documents, without a bank account, without stable housing or with a changeable income are the ones most likely to be excluded, and they are usually the ones the scheme was meant to help. A universal scheme also avoids stigma at the point of application and the political cost of taking money away from people who are only slightly above the line, which is why universal designs are often defended in terms of the scheme's overall social legitimacy.

questions.explanation: The item tests the defensible case for universal design, which rests on the administrative and exclusion costs of testing rather than on generosity. Where the test falls hardest, it is usually on the households the scheme exists to serve.
questions.hint: Ask what the eligibility test itself costs.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a growing number of veto players makes policy less predictable

stimulus.body: A source excerpt describes a country in which the same policy has been revised in different directions by each of five successive governments, and notes that each revision followed a successful challenge by a different body with standing to challenge it. The excerpt records that the underlying problem the policy addressed remained unfixed throughout.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what best explains the repeated revisions?

options.text: The five governments disagreed about goals, since each revision followed a different policy priority
options.misconception: substitutes goal disagreement for the blocking mechanism described

options.text: Multiple blocking actors make any settlement fragile, so each new government can reopen and reverse it
The policy was poorly drafted, since careful drafting prevents later revision
options.misconception: claims drafting skill forecloses political reversal

options.text: The unfixed problem caused the revisions, since voters rewarded action on it
options.misconception: reverses the causal direction the excerpt supports

questions.explanation: Each revision followed a successful challenge by a different blocking body, so the settlement lacked the protection of a single actor's consent and each new government could reopen it. The unchanged underlying problem is the evidence that the reversals produced churn rather than repair.
questions.hint: Ask what preceded each revision.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Identify when an advocate should press a proposal
questions.stem: A translator's note asks when an advocate holding a finished proposal should press it, given that the problem is widely recognised but no political opening has occurred.

options.text: Only after the problem has disappeared, since pressure then harms the case
options.misconception: invents a rule that the delay of an outdated case helps

options.text: Immediately, since public attention on its own is sufficient to force a decision
options.misconception: confuses attention with the opportunity to act

options.text: When the political context turns favourable, because attention without opportunity rarely produces adoption
Never, since a finished proposal cannot benefit from further revision
options.misconception: treats preparation as making revision unnecessary

questions.explanation: Recognition of a problem opens the first window but does not create the second, and proposals pressed on attention alone are typically overtaken by events or crowded out. The finished proposal should be held ready and pressed when the political context becomes favourable.
questions.hint: Distinguish the attention you have from the opening you need.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise the strength and weakness of incremental change
questions.stem: A translator's note records a decade of negotiated changes that kept a system working but never altered the rule causing the recurring problem. Which assessment is most defensible?

options.text: The changes were a mistake, since any partial measure delays action that should have been complete
options.misconception: judges partial measures as worse than none

options.text: The changes were worthless, since they never touched the underlying rule
options.misconception: discounts the improvements the note records

options.text: The changes were a success, since a working system is the only goal worth pursuing
options.misconception: treats continued operation as full resolution

options.text: The changes were worth making for what they fixed, yet they deferred the structural question and made it harder

questions.explanation: The decade of negotiated steps kept the system working and fixed specific grievances, so they had real value, but they left the rule that generates the problem in place and gave participants a stake in that arrangement. Both the achievement and the deferral belong in the assessment.
questions.hint: Weigh what the sequence fixed against what it postponed.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the limits of an information instrument

stimulus.body: A translator's note records a well-funded publicity campaign telling people to reduce heating use, which produced a measurable drop in reported intentions and no measurable change in consumption. It notes that households in the area were spending a large share of income on fuel and that no support scheme was available.

questions.stem: According to the translator's note, why did the information instrument underperform?

options.text: The campaign's message was poorly worded, since intentions fell less than expected
options.misconception: treats a change in intentions as evidence of poor wording

options.text: Knowing what to do was not the binding constraint, since households lacked the means to act on the advice
The information was not distributed widely enough, since too few people saw the campaign
options.misconception: contradicts the note that the campaign was well funded

options.text: Fuel prices fell during the period, so the consumption change reflects price rather than the campaign
options.misconception: invents a price movement the note does not report

questions.explanation: The campaign moved intentions but not behaviour, which indicates that information was not the binding constraint, and the note identifies the constraint directly in the household fuel bills and the absence of support. Information instruments shape choices only where the person has the capacity to act on them.
questions.hint: Ask what stopped households from acting on what they knew.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Explain how trust is built or eroded procedurally
questions.stem: Explain, for the translator's note, how the procedures an institution follows affect whether people trust it.

answer.exemplar: Trust is a judgement about how an institution will treat people, and that judgement is formed from observable procedure rather than from claims. When decisions are explained, when the reasoning is published, when an appeal route exists and is used, and when the same rules apply to the powerful as to everyone else, people have grounds to expect consistent treatment, and their trust in the body rises. Where a body gives no reasons, changes its practice without explanation or treats comparable cases differently, the same people have grounds to expect arbitrary treatment, and trust falls. Procedures are therefore the mechanism through which institutional trust is earned and lost.

questions.explanation: The item tests that trust rests on observed practice rather than on statements, since people infer future treatment from how cases have been handled. Consistent, explainable procedure is the mechanism that earns it.
questions.hint: Ask what people base their expectations on.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a source on the effect of participation on knowledge

stimulus.body: A source excerpt reports a programme in which people who took part in local decision-making later answered questions about how the council's budget worked substantially better than people who had only read the leaflets. The excerpt notes that participants had chosen to join and that leaflets had been sent to everyone, and asks the translator to avoid describing the programme as a training scheme.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what is the most accurate description of the programme?

options.text: The programme is a training scheme that happened to involve participation
options.misconception: contradicts the excerpt's instruction to the translator

options.text: The leaflets taught the budget, and participants simply read more of them
options.misconception: attributes the gap to reading rather than to participating

options.text: Participation itself supplied the knowledge, since the leaflets were sent to everyone and did not close the gap
The comparison is invalid, since participants were self-selected into the better informed
options.misconception: raises a valid caveat but leaves the reading of the excerpt unresolved

questions.explanation: Because the leaflets reached everyone and only participants improved, the knowledge came from the participation itself rather than from the information campaign, which is precisely why the excerpt asks the translator not to call it a training scheme. The selection caveat is real but does not describe what the excerpt is recording.
questions.hint: The leaflets reached everyone, so what differed?

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Assess the limits of a policy entrepreneur's ability to carry a reform
questions.stem: A single official prepared a proposal over six years and pressed it at the first opening. It was defeated, and the official lost the post. Which assessment is most defensible?

options.text: The official's loss of post shows the office was too powerful to attempt reform
options.misconception: reads an outcome as evidence about the constitution of the office

options.text: The defeat shows preparation was worthless, since a well-made proposal always wins
options.misconception: overstates the reliability of preparation alone

options.text: The defeat shows the official should have waited for a better window
options.misconception: ignores that the window was the point of waiting

options.text: Preparation and timing increase the odds of success but cannot supply the coalition and authority a reform needs

questions.explanation: Readiness and timing raise the probability that a proposal is heard, but a reform still requires the coalition, authority and support that no single advocate can supply, so a well-prepared proposal can still be defeated. The lesson is about limits rather than about wasted effort or bad timing.
questions.hint: Ask what preparation cannot provide on its own.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the argument that veto players improve policy quality
questions.stem: A translator's note records that a proposal took two years to pass and that the version finally adopted was narrower and contained a rights safeguard the original lacked. Which rendering of the passage is most defensible?

options.text: The delay is pure obstruction, since two years of waiting cannot be justified
options.misconception: ignores the safeguard the delay produced

options.text: The delay is both a cost in time and a source of the safeguard, so it should not be described as pure obstruction
The delay is pure benefit, since a longer process always yields better rules
options.misconception: assumes delay always improves outcomes

options.text: The passage is inconsistent, since a narrow outcome contradicts the claim of delay
options.misconception: treats a narrow result as evidence of contradiction

questions.explanation: The note records a real cost in the two-year timetable and a real benefit in the safeguard that appeared in the final text, so an accurate rendering holds both. Claiming either pure obstruction or pure benefit drops half of what the passage states.
questions.hint: Weigh the time cost against the safeguard.
